items.text: Six endings, each with one clear message
A step limit stops endless loops
Tool errors are observations, marked is_error
Never eval tool input: use an allow-list

captions.text: A loop that works on a good day is the easy part.
A good agent also behaves well on a bad day: when it can't finish, when a tool
fails, or when the input is dangerous.
This lesson is about stopping safely.
These habits will protect every agent you build from now on.
You'll list every way an agent loop can end.
You'll return tool errors to the model, instead of crashing.
And you'll build tools that refuse dangerous input.
A well-built agent knows exactly why it stopped.
Here are the six ways our calculator agent can end.
First, the good ending: the model answered.
Second, the step limit.
After a fixed number of turns, we stop, even if the model wants to continue.
Third, the budget, from Module 2.
When spending reaches the limit, we stop.
Fourth, a refusal: the model declined the request.
Fifth, the reply was cut off at max tokens.
And sixth, an API error that retries couldn't fix, like a rejected key.
For each ending, the user gets one clear message.
Never a traceback, and never a silent stop.
Why does the step limit matter so much?
A model can get stuck, asking for tools again and again.
Our fake API has a mode that does exactly that, so we can watch the limit work.
The fake keeps asking for one plus one.
After three turns, the agent stops and explains why, instead of running, and costing
money, forever.
Next, tool errors.
Tools will fail sometimes: the input is invalid, there's a division by zero, or a
unit doesn't exist.
Don't let that crash your program.
Instead, send the error message back to the model, as the tool's result.
Mark it with is error, true, so the model knows the call failed.
Now the model can read the error, fix its input, and try again.
And your step limit still caps how many times it can try.
Here's how the project does it.
Act runs one tool call and records it as a step.
If the tool raises a tool error, we don't crash.
The error message becomes the observation, marked as an error, and the loop carries
on.
Here the fake is scripted to send a broken expression first: eighteen x one point
one five.
The calculator returns an error, shown with an exclamation mark.
On the next turn the expression is fixed, and the agent finishes normally.
With a real model, this recovery isn't scripted.
The model reads the error message and corrects itself, which is why clear error
messages matter.
Now the most important safety rule in this lesson.
Tool input comes from the model, and the model's input comes, partly, from users.
So treat tool input like any untrusted input.
A calculator built with Python's eval function looks clever, but eval runs any
Python code at all, not just arithmetic.
Instead, our calculator parses the expression into a tree, and walks through it,
allowing only numbers, a few operators, and three functions.
Anything else is refused.
This script shows the difference, with a harmless example.
Given this text, eval happily imports the os module and runs a function: here it
prints the current folder.
It could just as easily delete files.
Our calculate function refuses it, and still does real maths perfectly.
Here's the idea.
Each kind of node in the tree must be explicitly allowed.
Numbers are allowed, and so are plus and minus signs.
Arithmetic operators are allowed, but only the ones in our list, and very large
powers are refused, so nobody can freeze your program with a giant calculation.
Three named functions are allowed: square root, absolute value, and round.
Everything else is refused.
That's an allow list: you list what's permitted, and refuse the rest.
It's much safer than trying to list everything that's dangerous.
One more thing.
In real projects, the Anthropic SDK has a tool runner that can run this loop for
you.
We built the loop by hand, so you understand exactly what any tool runner does
underneath.
In Module 5, you'll add more tools, validate their inputs, and ask a human for
confirmation before risky actions.
And in Module 7, you'll make agents reliable, with timeouts, token budgets, logging,
and tracing.
Pause and match each problem to the protection that handles it.
One.
The model keeps asking for tools, and never answers.
Two.
A user tries to sneak Python code into the calculator.
Three.
The model sends a letter x instead of a multiplication sign.
One: the step limit.
Two: the allow-list calculator, which refuses anything that isn't arithmetic.
Three: the tool error goes back to the model, which fixes its input.
Quick check.
Why send a tool's error back to the model, instead of raising an exception?
So the model can read it, fix its input, and continue.
And the step limit still caps how often it can try.
A loop can end six ways, and each gets one clear message.
A step limit stops endless loops.
Tool errors are observations, marked with is error.
And never eval tool input.
Use an allow list.
You now know every idea the project needs.
Next lesson, we build the smart calculator agent.
